title: Contractor Ghosted Me During House Flip: What to Do Right Now
excerpt: Getting ghosted by a contractor mid-flip can derail your entire project and eat into your profits. Here's exactly what to do when a contractor disappears and how to protect yourself from it happening again.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: contractor ghosted me during house flip what to do
metaDescription: Contractor ghosted you during a house flip? Follow these step-by-step actions to recover your project, protect your money, and finish your flip on time.
metaKeywords: contractor ghosted me during house flip what to do, contractor disappeared mid project, house flip contractor problems, how to handle contractor ghosting, real estate investor contractor tips, finding replacement contractor, contractor dispute resolution

sections.content: You hired a contractor, handed over a deposit, and now your calls are going straight to voicemail. Your flip is sitting half-finished. Your holding costs are climbing by the day. If a contractor ghosted you during a house flip, you're not alone — it happens to investors at every experience level. The good news is there are clear steps you can take right now to recover your project and limit the financial damage.
Step 1: Try Every Contact Method One More Time

Before you assume the worst, make one final documented attempt to reach your contractor through every channel available. Call, text, email, and even visit their listed business address if you have one. Sometimes a contractor goes dark because of a personal emergency, hospitalization, or a family crisis — not because they've deliberately abandoned your project. Send a written message that clearly states: 'I have not heard from you in X days. Please respond within 48 hours or I will assume you have abandoned the project and take appropriate action.' Keep screenshots of every attempt. This paper trail matters if you end up in small claims court or need to file a complaint.

Always send your final contact attempt via certified mail in addition to text and email. A certified letter creates a legal timestamp that proves you gave the contractor a fair chance to respond — and judges take that seriously.
Step 2: Assess the Damage and Document Everything

Once you've determined your contractor is truly gone, walk the property immediately with your phone camera rolling. Document every unfinished area — open walls, exposed plumbing, incomplete electrical, missing fixtures. Make a detailed list of what was promised in the contract versus what was actually completed. This documentation serves two purposes: it helps the next contractor give you an accurate bid, and it supports any legal or insurance claims you may need to file.

Use the free [Rehab Estimator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator) to quickly calculate what the remaining work should cost. This gives you a baseline so you're not walking into contractor interviews blind. Knowing your numbers also tells you whether the project is still profitable or whether you need to reconsider your exit strategy.
Step 3: Secure the Property

A half-finished renovation is a liability. Open structures invite theft, vandalism, and weather damage. If walls are open, cover them with plastic sheeting. Board up any broken windows or unsecured entry points. Change the locks immediately since your previous contractor likely still has a key. Call your insurance company to make sure your policy still covers the property in its current state — some policies have clauses about vacant or partially renovated homes that could void your coverage.
Step 4: Understand Your Legal Options
Review Your Contract First

Pull out your signed contract and read it carefully. Look for clauses about abandonment, breach of contract, and dispute resolution. Most solid contracts define abandonment as failing to show up or communicate for a set number of days — often 3 to 7 business days. If the contractor abandoned your project without completing what they were paid for, you may have grounds to recover your deposit or sue for damages.
Small Claims Court vs. Civil Lawsuit

For amounts under $10,000 (limits vary by state), small claims court is your fastest and cheapest option. You don't need a lawyer, the process is straightforward, and many investors win these cases when they have proper documentation. For larger disputes — say, a contractor took a $25,000 deposit and completed only $5,000 of work — you'll want to consult an attorney. Either way, your documented contact attempts, photos, and contract will be the foundation of your case.

items: File a complaint with your state's contractor licensing board — this can result in license suspension and often prompts a fast response from the contractor
Report the contractor to the Better Business Bureau and leave honest reviews on Google and Yelp to warn other investors
Contact your local real estate investor association (REIA) — they often have a vetted contractor list and can alert other members
If you paid by credit card, file a chargeback for the uncompleted portion of the work
Check whether your contractor carried a surety bond — if so, you can file a claim against the bond to recover losses

sections.content: Step 5: Find a Replacement Contractor Fast

Every day your property sits unfinished costs you money. The average house flip carries $1,500 to $3,000 per month in holding costs when you factor in insurance, utilities, taxes, and financing. Speed matters. Reach out to your local real estate investor network first — other investors in markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) often have reliable GC referrals they trust for fast-moving flip projects.

When interviewing replacement contractors, be upfront about the situation. Explain exactly what was done, what was left unfinished, and show them your documentation. Get at least three bids. Ask each contractor for references from similar rehab projects and actually call those references. Ask specifically: 'Did this contractor finish on time and on budget? Did they ever go quiet or become hard to reach?'

Structure your payment schedule with the replacement contractor so that no single payment exceeds the value of work completed. A common safe structure is 10% upfront, milestone-based payments, and 10-15% held back until final walkthrough and punch list completion.
How to Protect Yourself From Contractor Ghosting in Future Flips

Once you get through this flip, it's worth building systems that make contractor ghosting far less likely — and far less damaging when it does happen. Whether you're just starting out (check out this [real estate investing guide for beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners)) or you've been wholesaling for years (this [wholesaling real estate guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) covers contractor basics too), the fundamentals of contractor management are the same.

items: Always verify contractor licenses and insurance before signing anything — ask for certificates of insurance naming you as additionally insured
Use detailed written contracts that define abandonment, include a payment schedule tied to milestones, and outline penalties for delays
Never pay more than 10-15% upfront, no matter how much pressure you get to do otherwise
Require weekly progress photos or in-person check-ins, especially if you're investing out of state
Build a bench of 2-3 trusted contractors so you have backup options if one falls through
Run a background check and check court records for any prior contractor fraud cases

sections.content: The best time to protect yourself from a bad contractor is before you sign the contract. The second best time is right now — with better documentation, tighter payment terms, and a backup GC ready to go.
What If the Project Is No Longer Profitable?

Sometimes a contractor abandonment blows up your numbers entirely. If your rehab costs have increased significantly because of delays, duplicate labor, or damage caused by incomplete work, you need to reassess your exit strategy. Run the numbers again honestly. Can you still flip the property profitably? Should you consider renting it instead? Or would it make more sense to wholesale it to another investor as-is and cut your losses? There is no shame in pivoting — the worst move is throwing more money at a deal that no longer makes sense financially.
